And why need one mention other things, when we have a clear testimony to the argument in fevers themselves, which everyone daily says have sometimes become greater or less than one another, and sometimes that a man is feverish less or more, this one compared with the same man yesterday or today? Since, then, the 'more' according to quality is assumed to be said in this way, it is no wonder that, in a bath in which there is more substance of smoke, one says that both the quality and the activity have become more: if we name them properly, strong and more intense; if by catachresis, greater and more. For the smoke will clearly bite the eyes in proportion as it increases in substance too; so that, since the proper qualities and the activities always increase together with the substances, one would truly say that in such a bath the smoke is greatest.

Let it be supposed again, as we were saying, that there is some steam and smoke in the bath, while the proper substance of the air is greatest in proportion, being and becoming the analogue of the innate heat in animals; for now too it will be said that the proper heat in the bath is greatest. For one heat is kindled from the blood, another from the phlegm, another from the yellow or the black bile. In children, then, the substance of the blood is greatest according to the proportion of the mixture. For of this one must always remind, as though they were held fast by lethargy, those who babble such things as Lycus wrote; and the quality that increases with it is wholesome and friendly, not distressing and biting to those who touch, and so is the activity, according to which the digestions become neither nidorous nor acid, as in the case of phlegm.

Unit K18a.244-245 (K. XVIIIA 244–245). ENGLISH:
In all the ways, then, most noble Lycus, the innate heat is more in those who are growing, so that Hippocrates made no error, but rather you have been refuted as a malicious detractor. For you have shown from what you wrote that you were not at all introduced by teachers to understand anything of the Hippocratic doctrines, and that you openly bring charges against things of which you know nothing at all; and you were caught making a most ignorant counter-argument, attempting by means of it to overturn the constitution of every art; and, being ignorant of what Plato wrote on these matters, you often contradict yourself, doing harm to the young who, like you, are untrained in logical theory and do not know how to distinguish true arguments from false. On top of all this you were seen to be most audacious and at the same time a babbler, having undertaken to write exegeses of what was said by Hippocrates without first having learned it.
